Title: Spatiotemporal Reservoir Computing with a Reconfigurable Multifunctional Memristor Array

Spatiotemporal Reservoir Computing with a Reconﬁgurable
Multifunctional Memristor Array
Sungho Kim, Dong Hoon Shin, Wonho Choi, Sunwoo Cheong, Sung Keun Shim,
Soo Hyung Lee, Janguk Han, Yoon Ho Jang, Kunhee Son, Néstor Ghenzi,*
and Cheol Seong Hwang*
The existing physical implementations of reservoir computing are constrained
mainly by time-delay architectures that lack capabilities for spatial data
processing. This study presents a multifunctional memristor-based reservoir
computing system, the memristive echo state network (MESN), which
enables spatiotemporal computation within a single device crossbar array.
Utilizing a reconﬁgurable Ta/HfO2/RuO2 memristor, three distinct switching
modes are realized: stochastic for input masking, bistable for sigmoidal
activation, and analog for precise readout. A full in-memory implementation is
experimentally demonstrated using a one-transistor-one-resistor crossbar
array integrated with indium oxide thin-ﬁlm transistors. Spatial inference is
validated through cellular automata, conﬁrming reliable hardware operation.
High-level simulations based on the hardware results demonstrate the
performance of the proposed MESN, achieving high accuracy in predicting
the Lorenz attractor and classifying attention-deﬁcit/hyperactivity disorder.
The system also predicted the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, representing
the ﬁrst memristor-based reservoir to model complex spatiotemporal partial
diﬀerential equations. These results highlight the potential of multifunctional
memristor arrays for scalable in-memory spatiotemporal computing.

1. Introduction
Reservoir computing (RC), a framework
based on recurrent neural networks, of-
fers a practical and eﬃcient approach to
various machine learning tasks by signif-
icantly diminishing computational com-
plexity compared to conventional software-
based recurrent neural networks.[1,2] Con-
ventional RC consists of three main lay-
ers: the input, the reservoir, and the out-
put. The input layer transmits the cur-
rent state to the reservoir through ﬁxed
random weights, and the reservoir is a
randomly connected network composed of
multiple nonlinear nodes. The reservoir in-
tegrates state-dependent information and
projects it into a higher-dimensional space,
capturing various spatiotemporal patterns.
In achieving this goal, the randomness
and nonlinearity of the reservoir layer play
crucial roles. This high-dimensional re-
lationship is expressed through learning
weights in the fully connected network
of the output layer, thereby avoiding the
complex parameter optimization processes and mitigating the
vanishing gradient problem associated with backpropagation.[3,4]
Recently, RC has gained considerable attention for its poten-
tial in hardware implementation. In particular, physical reservoir
computing (PRC), which utilizes emerging memory devices like
memristors, employs a time-delay feedback-based approach.[5,6]
This method replaces the traditional randomly connected com-
plex network with a simpliﬁed nonlinear node and a delay loop.[7]
However, the intrinsic physical mechanisms during the PRC pro-
cess impose limitations, such as restricted relaxation times and
ﬁxed nonlinear functions, which constrain information process-
ing capacity.[8,9] To overcome these issues, PRC further utilized
memristor-driven multimodal and self-adaptive characteristics
and applied them to various tasks, including time-series predic-
tion, spatiotemporal pattern analysis, speech recognition, and
image classiﬁcation.[10–13] However, most eﬀorts have focused
on enhancing the temporal dynamics within time-delay feedback
systems unsuited for processing real-world data involving multi-
ple spatial dimensions.[14–18] Addressing these complexities and
expanding multidimensional spatial dynamics remains a signif-
icant challenge.[8,9,19]

Conventionally, software-based reservoirs expand spatiotem-
poral dimensions via vector-matrix multiplication (VMM), nat-
urally projecting inputs into high-dimensional states.[1] In con-
trast, time-delayed feedback RC encodes multiplexed temporal
inputs into the reservoir. This system generates virtual nodes in
a delay loop that utilizes inherent physical dynamics to transform
inputs into high-dimensional states.[7,10] Dynamic systems with
rich dynamics facilitate the discovery of new classiﬁcation bound-
aries through high-dimensional transformations. However, since
the virtual nodes within the reservoir and the encoded inputs are
multiplexed along the temporal axis, they are constrained to a
uniﬁed temporal topology. In particular, in memristor-based con-
ventional RC, the physical node and all reservoir nodes corre-
spond to a single memristive device, eﬀectively capturing tempo-
ral correlations (i.e., dx/dt) but not physically representing spatial
correlations between input channels (i.e., dy/dx).[20]
This study proposes an alternative reservoir structure that ef-
fectively reﬂects spatiotemporal relationships by utilizing three
distinct switching characteristics of memristor: stochastic switch-
ing, bistable switching, and analog switching. Inspired by the
echo state network architecture,[21] the proposed system incorpo-
rates three essential components implemented using a memris-
tive crossbar array (CBA): a stochastic mask, a nonlinear activa-
tion function, and a readout layer. For the stochastic mask, mul-
tiple random values are mapped in CBA as conductance and cor-
responding voltages are applied to represent the spatiotemporal
polynomials of multidimensional inputs through VMM. Here,
the term “mask” does not refer to temporal time-multiplexing as
in single-node RC systems, but rather to a spatially parallel ran-
dom projection matrix generated by the stochastic conductance
states. Each input vector is multiplied by this matrix, enabling
the reservoir to emulate a randomly connected network structure
without relying on sequential temporal encoding.
The nonlinear activation function adopts a widely used sig-
moid relationship. Speciﬁcally, the bistable switching behavior
of memristors follows a normal distribution of switching volt-
ages while the resulting states remain binary. Therefore, the
corresponding VMM readout current exhibits a sigmoidal be-
havior after applying a single voltage pulse. These two compo-
nents are sampled with one-shot mapping to generate a stochas-
tic mask and corresponding sigmoidal activation, making it suit-
able for real-time parallel computing. Lastly, the readout layer op-
erates as the output layer through analog-domain VMM applied
to the memristor devices with tunable and precisely mapped con-
ductance. Stochastically distributed conductance states, bistable
switching with voltage variation, and precisely tunable analog
states are necessary to implement the proposed memristive echo
state network (MESN).
Implementing diﬀerent data types typically requires distinct
device and circuit elements optimized for each data type; how-
ever, this approach often encounters challenges due to process
complexity and operational parameter mismatches. To overcome
these issues, this work utilizes the reconﬁgurable characteris-
tics of a multifunctional memristor to implement the MESN.
The MESN structure integrates three operational modes using
the multifunctionality of the Ta/HfO2/RuO2 (THR) memristor:
1) a stochastic mode to generate random distributions of con-
ductance, 2) a bistable mode with a probabilistic switching na-
ture for sigmoidal activation through binary-domain VMM, and
3) an analog mode for precise conductance mapping and read-
out via analog-domain VMM. The proposed network structure is
validated in a one-transistor-one-resistor (1T1R) conﬁguration[22]
with integrated thin-ﬁlm transistors (TFTs) featuring an In2O3
channel and a THR memristor. This 1T1R architecture and pro-
posed MESN were validated through experimental implemen-
tation of cellular automata. Furthermore, utilizing the multi-
functional characteristics of the fabricated hardware, the MESN
demonstrated the capacity to handle both temporal and spatial
dynamics eﬀectively. Its versatility was validated through tasks
such as predicting the Lorenz 63 system, classifying attention-
deﬁcit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and predicting partial dif-
ferential equations (PDEs). For the Lorenz benchmark predic-
tion, the reservoir demonstrated the ability to predict chaotic mul-
tivariate dynamics accurately. In the ADHD classiﬁcation task,
the reservoir eﬀectively generated diverse and high-dimensional
states from a limited dataset. Predicting PDE requires tempo-
ral and spatial correlation information from prior states. The
proposed reservoir was further explored to feasibly predict the
Kuramoto–Shivashinsky (KS) PDE equation with a memristor-
based PRC system, which has not been reported yet. The MESN
demonstrates the potential for breakthroughs that surpass the
limitations of time-delay feedback, which is commonly employed
in conventional PRC implementations. Figure S1 and Table
S2, and Note S1 (Supporting Information) provide a schematic
overview of the proposed architecture and a conceptual compari-
son to conventional reservoir systems.
2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Multifunctional Memristive CBA for MESN
The unit memristor for the MESN architecture should ex-
hibit multifunctional switching behavior to function as various
layer components. Moreover, the operational parameters (switch-
ing voltage and state resistance) must be clearly distinguished
between diﬀerent switching modes, while uniform operation
within each mode must also be ensured. For these requirements,
this work utilizes the THR memristor for the unit devices of the
proposed MESN. The RuO2 bottom electrode supplies oxygen to
the HfO2 dielectric layer, while the Ta top electrode provides oxy-
gen vacancies that contribute to the formation of the switching
ﬁlament within the HfO2 layer. Due to the diﬀerent roles of these
electrodes, as reported in previous studies, the THR memristor
undergoes a two-step reset process, enabling the device to be re-
conﬁgured into various switching modes.[23] Utilizing these di-
verse and clearly distinguishable switching characteristics, which
have already been employed in data mining, stochastic comput-
ing, and logic computing applications, the THR memristor is ide-
ally suited to implement each functional element required in the
MESN pipeline.[24–27]

Figure 1d–f schematically illustrate the switching mechanisms
of the THR memristor under its three distinct operational modes.
In the bistable mode shown in Figure 1d, the conductive ﬁla-
ment undergoes complete dissolution through interfacial reac-
tions with both the top and bottom electrodes, allowing for a clear
transition between high and low resistance states. In contrast, the
stochastic mode depicted in Figure 1e involves an incomplete re-
set process, where the ﬁlament is partially disrupted. This partial
rupture results in a random ﬁlamentary structure, leading to a
broad distribution of conductance states. Lastly, the analog mode
illustrated in Figure 1f operates by applying reset voltages only up
to the threshold before abrupt rupture, allowing for a gradual and
controllable modulation of the ﬁlament. This enables ﬁne adjust-
ment of conductance, supporting continuous and programmable
analog switching behavior. The performance of each mode and
its application to the proposed RC network, including random
masking, sigmoidal activation, and conductance tuning, are dis-

tive array was fabricated by integrating the THR memristor with
an In2O3 channel TFT, featuring a channel length and width
of 0.7 and 15 μm, respectively, serving as a selector. Figure 2a

ture schematic diagram (bottom panel) of the fabricated 16 by 16
1T1R active array, where the THR memristor has a cell area of
16 μm2. In this structure, an In2O3-channel TFT was integrated

terminal to the bottom electrode through an Al2O3 interlayer di-

ditional switching characteristics of the 1T1R unit, validating its
role as a selection device within the CBA.

the MESN. The voltage parameters designated for each mode

Figure 2f–h present the results of implementing a sigmoid ac-
tivation function using the bistable mode array. Figure 2f illus-
trates the 1T1R unit cell operation method for bistable switching
and sigmoidal readout. In the bistable mode, the THR memristor
cells probabilistically switch to LRS when applying bistable sam-
pling voltage (VD,Bist) to HRS. In this case, the gate voltage (VG,Bist)
is set to 2 V to ensure the compliance current for the set opera-
tion. When these switched cells in a single string are simultane-
ously read with a given VD,R of 0.1 V, the LRS cells contribute to
the total output current (IOUT), while the contribution from HRS
cells remains negligible. With the minimal LRS variation, the out-
put current becomes proportional to the number of LRS cells.
Figure 2g presents the distribution of the set voltage for bistable
mode cells within a column in the CBA (16 devices). When a 16
by 1 subarray is driven according to the method in Figure 2f, the
VMM current output, governed by the bistable switching of the
cells based on the applied VD,Bist, follows a sigmoidal curve be-
cause the set switching probability follows the Gaussian distri-
bution. Figure 2h illustrates the output sigmoidal relationship,
demonstrating that one-shot sigmoid mapping and output gen-
eration are achievable within a single column of bistable mode
in CBA.

2.4. PDE KS Prediction
The Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) system is a fourth-order PDE
that models diﬀusive–thermal instabilities. Unlike the Lorenz
system, the KS system coexists with low-order time and high-
order spatial derivatives. The competition between the time and
space function derivatives leads to chaotic phase gradients in
both time and space, resulting in the absence of analytical so-
lutions and reliance on numerical approximations. It is challeng-
ing to perform data processing that accounts for both the con-
tinuously changing rate of time and spatial changes within an
integrated system, so most PRC research has shown unsatisfac-
tory results.[33,34] The potential of the suggested MESN system is
further explored for the KS problem using the numerical anal-
ysis values as ground truth to predict and grid the KS system.
The detailed grid discretized process is described in the experi-
mental section, and the overall process is similar to the Lorenz
63 attractor. Analog precision resembling the analog mode char-
acteristics, and 2500 reservoir nodes were used for prediction. A
stochastic mask array was created using 500 random masks with
a standard deviation of ﬁve. Figure 5a illustrates the short-term
prediction results following training for 800 time steps. The y-
axis represents the spatial domain, and the x-axis denotes Lya-
punov times. The color bar label indicates the variable 𝑢. The
error plot in Figure 5a indicates that the MESN accurately pre-
dicts up to 4 Lyapunov times. Figure S10 (Supporting Informa-
tion) further shows that the MESN accurately predicts up to 5
Lyapunov times, achieving a consistently low NRMSE below 0.1.
It performs similarly to software-based ESN, assuming the same
number of reservoir nodes, which can accurately predict up to
3–4 Lyapunov times.[33] Figure 5b illustrates the results of long-
term prediction for 4500 time steps. Although deviations emerge
over time due to system evolution, the chaotic behavior of the
KS system is preserved. Figure 5c shows the average frequency
spectrum in an arbitrary spatial dimension (33rd in this case)
for quantitative analysis of the long-term forecast. The long-term
forecast was divided into 500 time-step intervals, and the power
spectra obtained by Fourier transforming each interval were av-
eraged. The close match between the frequency spectrum of the
ground truth and the predictions validates the stability and learn-

ics.

3. Conclusion
This work presents a multifunctional memristor-based reservoir
computing architecture, MSEN, that enables spatiotemporal in-
formation processing within a compact and reconﬁgurable in-
memory system. All key functions of a reservoir network, in-
cluding random input masking, nonlinear activation, and analog-
domain readout, were implemented directly in hardware by inte-
grating stochastic, bistable, and analog switching modes within
a single Ta/HfO2/RuO2 memristor device. The fabricated 1T1R
crossbar array, constructed with In2O3 channel thin-ﬁlm transis-
tors, feasibly demonstrated spatial computation through a cel-
lular automata task, validating the feasibility of layer-wise in-
memory operations. Beyond hardware demonstration, the pro-
posed architecture was evaluated through large-scale simulations
across spatiotemporal benchmarks using the hardware parame-
ters extracted from the 16 by 16 1T1R CBA. The MESN’s abil-
ity to eﬃciently model both temporal and spatial correlations
was validated in various tasks. In multivariate Lorenz system
prediction, the MESN achieved NRMSE of 0.077 up to 5 Lya-
punov times, demonstrating precise short-term forecasting of
chaotic dynamics. Nondeterministic tasks such as ADHD clas-
siﬁcation achieved an accuracy of 83.3%, eﬀectively mitigating
overﬁtting in data-limited scenarios. Moreover, the MESN cap-
tured short- and long-term behavior in the chaotic Kuramoto–
Sivashinsky PDE, representing a memristor-based physical reser-
voir’s ﬁrst feasible PDE modeling. These results underscore the
potential of multifunctional, nonvolatile memristor arrays to sur-
pass the limitations of time-delay-based physical reservoir com-
puting. By oﬀering a uniﬁed and reconﬁgurable platform capa-
ble of spatial and temporal modeling, this work paves the way
for hardware-software co-design in next-generation neuromor-
phic systems, enabling eﬃcient and real-time analysis of complex
dynamic data.

Cellular automata were a discrete computation model, ﬁrst intro-

according to a ﬁxed rule based on its current state and neighbors.[36] This

ADHD was a chronic neurobehavioral disorder characterized by inatten-

connectome, and the time-series data of each patient were divided into
10 segments, each patient therefore has 10 connectomes in this analysis.
Each connectome was independently classiﬁed by the readout layer into
ADHD or control. The ﬁnal label for a patient was determined by hard vot-
ing. If more than half of the ten connectomes were classiﬁed as ADHD,
the patient was labeled as ADHD; otherwise, the patient was labeled as a
control.

Performance Metrics—Lyapunov Exponents (𝜆max) and Lyapunov Time:
The Lyapunov exponent was a widely used metric in chaotic system dy-
namics that measures the rate at which two initially close states diverge ex-
ponentially. A larger Lyapunov exponent indicates more rapid divergence,
implying stronger chaotic behavior and greater diﬃculty in prediction. For
the Lorenz 63 attractor, 𝜆max = 0.91 and for the KS equation studied in
this work, 𝜆max = 0.043. Lyapunov time was a metric that quantiﬁes the
timescale over which a chaotic dynamical system remains predictable. It
was computed as the reciprocal of the largest 𝜆max of the system.
